title: Bits of Halley's Comet behind doomsday panic blaze over the US tonight
excerpt: Pieces of Halley's Comet are set to blaze across the skies tonight, but the famous comet has a dark history of fueling chilling doomsday fears.
content:
Pieces of Halley's Comet, the celestial visitor that once sparked chilling doomsday panic, are set to blaze across America's skies overnight.

The comet leaves a trail of dust and tiny fragments as it travels around the sun. 

Every October, Earth passes through that debris, which burns up in our atmosphere to produce the shooting stars known as the Orionid meteor shower.

The annual display peaks overnight, with viewers under clear, dark skies potentially spotting 10 to 20 meteors per hour as the particles travel at roughly 41 miles per second.

The best viewing conditions come in the hours before dawn, away from streetlights and other sources of light pollution.

But the comet's appearance in 1910 inspired terror after astronomers detected cyanogen, a toxic gas, in its tail.

Reports fueled fears that Earth's passage through the tail could wipe out life, despite scientists' reassurances that it posed no danger.

Sellers seized on the anxiety, marketing 'anti-comet pills,' gas masks and supposedly protective umbrellas, while some frightened residents sealed their doors and windows to keep the gas out.

The comet's appearance in 1910 (pictured) inspired terror after astronomers detected cyanogen, a toxic gas, in its tail

For Americans hoping to catch tonight's display, a bright moon could obscure some of the fainter meteors. Conditions will improve after moonset, although clouds and light pollution could also reduce the number visible.

No telescope or binoculars are needed. NASA recommends allowing around 30 minutes for your eyes to adjust to the darkness and reclining comfortably to take in as much of the sky as possible.

Although the meteors appear to originate near the constellation Orion, they can streak across any part of the sky, so viewers should avoid concentrating on a single spot.

Some Orionids leave glowing trails that linger for seconds or even minutes, while occasional brighter meteors can produce dramatic flashes known as fireballs.

Anyone who misses tonight's peak could still catch shooting stars on surrounding nights, with the shower remaining active until November 7.

The spectacle offers a very different experience from the fear that surrounded Halley's appearance more than a century ago.

In early 1910, astronomers at the Yerkes Observatory in Wisconsin spent weeks studying the approaching comet. 

On February 7, they announced that they had detected cyanogen in its tail.

Every October, Earth passes through that debris, which burns up in our atmosphere to produce the shooting stars known as the Orionid meteor shower

The discovery attracted the attention of French astronomer Camille Flammarion, who speculated that the gas could theoretically 'impregnate the atmosphere and possibly snuff out all life on the planet.'

The New York Times published an article headlined 'Comet's Poisonous Tail,' and other newspapers amplified the alarming possibility despite reassurances from scientists.

Some German farmers declined to plant crops that spring because they believed they would die before the harvest, according to the Science History Institute.

In early 1910 (pictured), astronomers at the Yerkes Observatory in Wisconsin spent weeks studying the approaching comet. On February 7, they announced that they had detected cyanogen in its tail

A Los Angeles broker sold 'comet insurance,' promising $500 to the families of anyone killed by Halley's passage.

The institute also reports that suicide deaths in at least four countries were attributed to the panic, while some frightened people lowered themselves into wells to escape the supposed threat.

Researchers studying drawings in a Puerto Rican cave have suggested that a family may also have sheltered underground during the comet's visit. 

The artwork includes a comet above a tomb-like structure and inscriptions dated May 23, 1910.

Earth passed safely through Halley's tail that May. The material was far too thinly dispersed to produce the catastrophe some had feared.

Halley's Comet itself last appeared in 1986 and is expected to return in 2061. Until then, its scattered debris continues to produce the annual Orionid display.
